::: {.callout-note .se-question appearance="simple"}
## The question

[How to calculate $\int(5x)^4e^{-2x}dx$ without using IBP?](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/1151144/how-to-calculate-int5x4e-2xdx-without-using-ibp), asked by [Richard](https://math.stackexchange.com/users/214154/richard) on Mathematics Stack Exchange (2015-02-16; [CC BY-SA 3.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/)):

> How do I integrate this? 
>
> (UPDATE: Sorry, I should have clarified that I've been told to use the gamma function and not just integration by parts, also that this is a definite integral.)
>
> $$\int_{x=0}^\infty (5x)^4e^{-2x}dx$$
>
> I know that that  $\displaystyle\int_0^\infty w^se^{-w}dw = s!=\Gamma(s+1)$, and I've been told to apply this fact, but I can't figure out how to apply this second equation to the first equation above. 
>
> I can simplify the first equation as follows:
>
> $$= 5^4\int_{x=0}^\infty x^4e^{-2x}\,dw$$
>
> Then if I let $w = 2x$, I can get to:
>
> $$= \frac{5^4}{2^4} \int_{x=0}^\infty w^4  e^{-w} \, dw$$
>
> But I'm not sure what to do next!
:::

You are so close!  Notice that since $w=2x$,
$$\frac{5^4}{2^4}\int_{x=0}^\infty w^4 e^{-w}{dw} = \frac{5^4}{2^4}\int_{{\color{green}w}=0}^\infty w^4 e^{-w}{dw}$$
And now you substitute your known fact
$$\frac{5^4}{2^4}\int_{w=0}^\infty w^4 e^{-w}{dw} = \frac{5^4}{2^4}4!$$
